summary: Dexibuprofen is the pharmacologically active S-(+)-enantiomer of racemic ibuprofen, a propionic acid NSAID with analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects (and platelet inhibition). It is licensed in the EU (e.g. Seractil) for symptomatic relief of pain and inflammation in osteoarthritis, primary dysmenorrhoea, and other mild-to-moderate pain such as musculoskeletal or dental pain. The usual adult dose is 600-900 mg/day in up to three divided doses, maximum single dose 400 mg and maximum 1200 mg/day; the dose is roughly half the corresponding racemic ibuprofen dose. Like all NSAIDs it carries GI ulcer/bleeding risk, a small dose-dependent cardiovascular thrombotic risk, renal and hepatic risks, and rare severe skin reactions; it is contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy. It is not FDA-approved in the United States.
indications: Symptomatic relief of pain and inflammation associated with osteoarthritis
Acute symptomatic treatment of pain during menstrual bleeding (primary dysmenorrhoea)
Symptomatic treatment of other forms of mild to moderate pain, such as musculoskeletal or dental pain

moa: Dexibuprofen is the active S-(+)-enantiomer of ibuprofen and inhibits prostaglandin synthesis through non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibition, producing analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects. It also inhibits platelet aggregation.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dexibuprofen, other NSAIDs, or any excipient
History of asthma, bronchospasm, rhinitis, nasal polyps, urticaria or angioedema precipitated by aspirin/NSAIDs
Active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage, or GI bleeding/perforation related to prior NSAID use
Severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min) or severe hepatic impairment
Third trimester of pregnancy (from the beginning of the 6th month)
Active Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis; cerebrovascular or other active bleeding
relative: Hypertension and/or cardiac failure, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial or cerebrovascular disease
Concomitant anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids or SSRIs
First and second trimesters of pregnancy
monitor: Full blood count with long-term use

preg: Avoid in the first and second trimesters unless clearly necessary (NSAIDs may increase miscarriage and cardiac malformation risk; from about week 20 risk of fetal renal impairment and oligohydramnios). CONTRAINDICATED in the third trimester (from the beginning of the 6th month) - risk of premature closure/constriction of the ductus arteriosus, pulmonary hypertension, fetal renal dysfunction, and inhibition of labour/uterine contractions.
lact: Breastfeeding is possible if the dose is low and the treatment short; for higher-dose or longer-term use, consider early weaning.
renal: Reduce the starting dose in mild-to-moderate renal impairment and monitor renal function; use particular caution with diuretics, ACE inhibitors, dehydration and in the elderly. Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min). Risk of interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, papillary necrosis and acute renal failure.
hepatic: Use a lower dose with close monitoring in mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment; monitor liver parameters and discontinue if a relevant/persistent rise occurs. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin) and antiplatelets/thrombolytics - increased bleeding risk; monitor coagulation/INR
Other NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin (analgesic doses) - additive GI ulceration/bleeding; avoid combining
High-dose methotrexate (>=15 mg/week) - increased methotrexate toxicity; avoid
moderate: Corticosteroids and SSRIs - increased GI bleeding risk
ACE inhibitors/angiotensin-II antagonists and diuretics - reduced antihypertensive effect and increased risk of acute renal failure (especially elderly/dehydrated)
Lithium - reduced renal clearance, raised levels; monitor
Digoxin - possible raised plasma levels; low-dose aspirin cardioprotection may be reduced
minor: Phenytoin (possible raised levels); CYP2C8/2C9 inducers (rifampicin, phenobarbital) may reduce effect; sulphonylureas; zidovudine; pemetrexed (avoid NSAID around dosing)
interactions.food: Take with or after food to reduce GI irritation; a high-fat meal slightly delays absorption without clinically relevant effect on total absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - increases gastrointestinal adverse effects and bleeding risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise liver enzymes, affect renal function tests and serum potassium; prolongs bleeding time.

serious: Peptic ulcer, GI bleeding or perforation (sometimes fatal, especially in the elderly)
Arterial thrombotic events (myocardial infarction, stroke) - small increased risk at high dose/long-term use
Acute renal failure, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, papillary necrosis
rare: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP
Haematological reactions (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, aplastic/haemolytic anaemia)

monitoring: Renal function (especially in the elderly, pre-existing impairment, or with diuretics/ACE inhibitors)
Full blood count with long-term therapy
INR/coagulation if on anticoagulants; lithium levels; methotrexate counts
counsel: Take with or after food and use the lowest dose for the shortest time needed
Stop and seek help for black/bloody stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, chest pain, breathlessness, or a spreading rash/blistering
Tell your doctor about all other medicines - especially blood thinners, aspirin, steroids and antidepressants
Do not use in late pregnancy; tell your doctor if you may be pregnant
This is the active half of ibuprofen, so the dose looks lower than ordinary ibuprofen
pk: Analgesic effect within ~30-60 minutes of an oral dose
Maximum plasma concentration at approximately 2 hours (delayed slightly by a high-fat meal)
Short - dosed up to 3 times daily; eliminated mainly renally (~90%) after hepatic metabolism
pearls: Dexibuprofen is the active S-(+)-enantiomer of ibuprofen - dose is roughly HALF the racemic ibuprofen dose (1200 mg dexibuprofen ~ 2400 mg ibuprofen)
Same NSAID class risks as ibuprofen: GI bleeding/perforation and a small dose-dependent thrombotic (MI/stroke) risk - avoid in severe heart failure and uncontrolled hypertension
Contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy (ductus arteriosus closure)
Consider gastroprotection (PPI) in high-risk patients; lowest effective dose, shortest duration
Not FDA-approved in the United States - EU/SmPC product
missed: Take a missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Acute toxicity is generally low, with symptoms within about 4 hours (more likely above ~80-100 mg/kg ibuprofen-equivalent). Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, drowsiness and headache; severe cases may show GI bleeding, hypotension, hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, seizures, renal impairment, respiratory depression or coma. Management is supportive/symptomatic with no specific antidote; activated charcoal for significant recent ingestion. Forced diuresis, haemodialysis and haemoperfusion are not useful due to high protein binding.
